Is Baltimore a city or part of a county?

Baltimore is an independent city, separate from any county since 1851. Baltimore County almost surrounds it, and Anne Arundel County borders it to the south. The Census Bureau treats it as a county equivalent, which is why city agencies handle jobs a county would elsewhere, from tax collection to land records.

The city sits on the Patapsco River near where it empties into the Chesapeake Bay. It covers 92.05 square miles, of which 80.95 are land. The fall line between the Piedmont Plateau and the Atlantic Coastal Plain splits it into a lower city and an upper city, with a high point of about 480 feet near Pimlico.

What are Baltimore's main areas and neighborhoods?

The city is divided into nine regions that match police districts: North, Northeast, East, Southeast, South, Southwest, West, Northwest and Central. Downtown and the Inner Harbor are in Central.

  • South and Southeast: Federal Hill, Fells Point, Canton, Little Italy and Locust Point.
  • North: Roland Park, Hampden, Charles Village and Mount Washington.

Tens of thousands of rowhouses give the city its look. Rowhouses became the dominant house type early in the 19th century, and many have brick or formstone fronts. Formstone was patented in 1937 by Albert Knight.

How has Baltimore's population and economy changed?

Baltimore reached its peak population of 949,708 in the 1950 census and counted 585,708 in 2020. Heavy industry declined, and the city moved toward a service economy, with Inner Harbor redevelopment starting in the 1970s.

Johns Hopkins Hospital and Johns Hopkins University are the top employers. Other major companies named include Under Armour, T. Rowe Price, McCormick & Company and Royal Farms. Services provide about 31% of jobs.

The Port of Baltimore dates to 1706 and serves more than 50 ocean carriers. On March 26, 2024, the Francis Scott Key Bridge collapsed after a container ship struck it.

What is the climate in Baltimore, and what does it do to a house?

Baltimore has a humid subtropical climate. The July daily average is about 80.7 degrees, January averages 35.8 degrees, and annual precipitation at BWI airport is 45 inches, with about 19 inches of snow a season.

The record high is 108 degrees (July 22, 2011), and the record low is minus 7 degrees (January 22, 1984). That is a 115-degree spread between the record extremes, and a roof or heating system here sees all of it.

How do people get around Baltimore?

Light RailLink opened in April 1992 and runs from Hunt Valley through downtown to Glen Burnie and BWI Airport. Metro SubwayLink opened in November 1983 and connects downtown near Johns Hopkins Hospital with Owings Mills.

MARC's Brunswick, Camden and Penn lines link the city with Washington's Union Station, and Amtrak serves Penn Station. BWI Airport is about 10 miles south in Anne Arundel County. The Fort McHenry Tunnel carries I-95 and opened in 1985, and the Jones Falls Expressway (I-83) was the first interstate built in the city.

How is real property tax billed in Baltimore?

Baltimore mails real property tax bills every July 1. The city rate is $2.248 per $100 of assessed value, and the state rate of $0.112 per $100 is collected on the same bill.

  • Bills are due on receipt, with a one-half percent discount if paid by July 31.
  • Interest and penalties begin after October 1.
  • Late payments accrue 1 percent interest plus a 1 percent penalty per month.
  • Owner-occupied homes can pay in two equal parts, the second before January 1 with a small added fee.
  • A pending appeal does not excuse late payment, but a successful one brings a refund with interest.

The City applies a Homestead Tax Credit that caps yearly growth in taxable value for owner-occupied homes at 4%. State assessments set the values: in the January 1, 2026 reassessment, residential values in Baltimore City rose 13.4% over 2023, phased in over three years.

What is the Baltimore tax sale calendar?

Baltimore holds a tax sale every May, and a house can become eligible when a non-owner-occupied property owes $250 or an owner-occupied one owes $750.

WhenWhat happens

First week of AprilSecond notice, covering amounts through April 30
April 30Last day to pay to avoid the sale
Third week of MayAnnual tax sale, normally
Six months after saleBuyer may sue to foreclose redemption on non-owner-occupied homes
Nine months after saleSame right for owner-occupied homes

The city says it cannot waive the fees and costs that state law sets for the bidder. A Tax Sale Deferral Program protects a property for one year without erasing the debt. If a homeowner falls behind, paying off the balance by April 30 is the cleanest way out, and a sale to a cash buyer who clears the lien at settlement is another.

How many vacant houses does Baltimore have?

As of January 28, 2022, Baltimore had 15,032 vacant houses, about 13,560 of them privately owned. That number was announced when the mayor ordered a 30-day review of how city agencies handle vacants, after a fire and collapse at a vacant house on South Stricker Street killed three firefighters.

The city's housing department files receivership cases against neglected vacants, and it was on track to file nearly 500 in that fiscal year. An owner of a vacant or inherited house can avoid that process by selling the property before a case is filed.

What does it cost to transfer a Baltimore house?

The city transfer tax is 1.5% of the consideration, and the state transfer tax is another 0.5%, for a total of 2%. The recordation tax is $5 for each $500 of consideration.

Transfers in Baltimore are processed in person at the Abel Wolman Municipal Building, Room 1B, 200 N. Holliday Street. Document processing is open to the public on Mondays and Wednesdays only. Each turn takes up to three documents, and each deed can cover up to three properties.

  • Bring a lien certificate, an original signed and notarized deed, an intake sheet, a settlement sheet copy and the contract of sale.
  • Pay open liens in full before signing in.
  • Use separate checks payable to the Director of Finance for city transfer tax, recordation tax and any yield tax.
  • Simplifile is available for e-recording.

What must a Baltimore seller disclose?

A seller of a house with four or fewer units must give the buyer a state disclosure or disclaimer statement on or before the contract is signed (Maryland Real Property Code 10-702). The disclaimer states that the property is being sold as-is, except for known latent defects.

Sales by lenders after foreclosure, sheriff and tax sales, and fiduciary transfers from estates and trusts are exempt. If a buyer is not given the form on time, the buyer can rescind within five days after receiving it.

Baltimore City Public Schools run the city's public schools, and about 100,000 college students attend the city's 10 accredited colleges and universities.

More questions about Baltimore, MD

What is the Baltimore City property tax rate?

The city rate is $2.248 per $100 of assessed value, plus a $0.112 state rate on the same bill. A $100,000 assessment produces $2,248 in city tax.

When are Baltimore property taxes due?

Bills are mailed July 1 and due on receipt. Interest and penalties start after October 1, and a one-half percent discount applies if you pay by July 31.

What is the Baltimore transfer tax?

The city transfer tax is 1.5% and the state transfer tax is 0.5%, a total of 2% of the consideration. Recordation tax is $5 per $500.

When does the Baltimore tax sale happen?

It is normally held in the third week of May. April 30 is the last day to pay taxes and avoid the sale.

How much unpaid tax makes a Baltimore house eligible for tax sale?

The city lists $250 or more for non-owner-occupied property and $750 or more for owner-occupied homes.

Where do I record a deed in Baltimore?

At the Abel Wolman Municipal Building, 200 N. Holliday Street, Room 1B, on Mondays and Wednesdays, or with e-recording through Simplifile. Bring the lien certificate and notarized original deed.

Can I sell a vacant Baltimore house as-is?

Yes. Maryland allows an as-is sale with a disclaimer statement. Any liens, tax debt or open code notices still have to be paid or settled at closing.

What is Frederick, Maryland, and how is it laid out?

Frederick is the seat of Frederick County and the second-largest incorporated city in Maryland after Baltimore. It sits about 46 miles west of Baltimore and roughly 50 miles north of Washington, D.C., where Catoctin Mountain meets the Piedmont.

The city covers 24.56 square miles. The Monocacy River runs east of town, and Carroll Creek runs through it. The 2020 Census counted 78,171 people, up from 65,239 in 2010, a gain of 19.8% in ten years. That growth means plenty of newer subdivisions on the edges, and an older core downtown where the houses are far older than the rest of the housing stock.

What is Frederick's history, and why does it matter to a seller?

Daniel Dulany laid out Frederick Town in 1745, and Frederick County was formed in 1748 with the town as its seat.

Schifferstadt, built in 1756, is described by Wikipedia as probably the oldest standing house in the city. In 1861 Frederick briefly served as Maryland's capital while the legislature debated secession, and in July 1864 the Battle of Monocacy was fought just southeast of town. The C&O Canal began operating and the B&O Frederick Branch was completed in 1831.

If you own a house in the center, its age can bring its own questions: older wiring, plaster, small closets, stone or brick foundations and the like. A buyer will price those in, and a cash buyer will usually look at the structure as is rather than ask you to modernize first.

Who are the biggest employers around Frederick?

Fort Detrick is the largest employer in Frederick County, with 10,827 employees in 2025, followed by the county school system. The list leans heavily toward federal, biomedical and public-sector jobs.

  • Fort Detrick (U.S. Army bioscience and communications): 10,827
  • Frederick County Board of Education: 7,433
  • Frederick Health: 3,360
  • Frederick County Government: 2,810
  • Leidos Biomedical Research: 2,370
  • Frederick Community College: 1,369
  • Frederick City Government: 977
  • AstraZeneca: 750

The Riverside Research Park on the east side includes the National Cancer Institute's Frederick National Laboratory and Charles River Labs. Downtown has about 600 businesses and organizations with nearly 5,000 jobs. Wikipedia credits federal investment and the growth of the Washington metro area for much of the city's growth.

How does the Historic District affect selling or fixing up a house?

If your house is inside Downtown Frederick's historic district, exterior changes need approval from the city's Historic Preservation Commission before work begins. The commission's guidance says all exterior alterations require approval unless they are on a minor rehabilitation list.

Items the guide names include:

  • Sheds, fences, gates, walls and paving, including patios and driveways
  • Repair or replacement of doors and windows
  • Additions, porches, stoops, and outdoor HVAC or utility equipment
  • New lighting fixtures

Some projects are approved by Planning staff, while larger ones go to a Commission hearing with a sign posted at the site. The brochures do not define the exact district boundary, so call the city's Planning Department to find out whether your street is covered. For a seller, the trade-off is simple: fixing up a historic house before listing can take longer than you expect, and a buyer who plans to renovate will need to account for the review. Selling as is avoids starting any of that work yourself.

Does Carroll Creek or the weather create flood risk for a Frederick house?

Parts of Frederick have a documented flood history. Carroll Creek Park began in the late 1970s as a flood control project after floods in 1972 and 1976, and it now serves as a downtown park with an amphitheater and pedestrian bridges.

The climate is humid subtropical, with an average annual precipitation of 43.52 inches and average snowfall of 16.5 inches. Wikipedia lists a July mean daily maximum of 88.6 degrees F and a January mean daily minimum of 26.5 degrees F. The record high of 109 degrees F on July 10, 1936, is the highest ever recorded in Maryland. Heavy summer rain and winter freezes can mean basement moisture, gutter problems and roof wear, so those are the first places a buyer's inspector will look.

Check FEMA's flood map for your exact address and keep any flood insurance paperwork handy for the buyer.

How do I get around Frederick, and why does commute time matter?

Frederick sits on a junction of I-70, I-270, US 15, US 40 and US 340, with MD 80, MD 144 and MD 355 inside the area. Commuting to the Washington region is a major reason people buy here, so a house near a ramp or a MARC station may attract different buyers from one on a quiet street.

MARC commuter rail runs to Washington, D.C., express bus route 991 goes to Shady Grove Metro, and TransIT runs local buses. Frederick Municipal Airport (FDK) handles general aviation with a mile-long main runway. Schools come from Frederick County Public Schools, and higher education includes Frederick Community College, Hood College and a campus of Mount St. Mary's University.

What are the property tax and closing steps for a Frederick seller?

Frederick County mails annual and semi-annual tax bills in July, and they are posted online by July 1. Annual bills are due September 30, and semi-annual bills split into September 30 and December 31 installments. Interest begins on October 1 at 1% per month on unpaid balances.

Paying in July earns a 1% discount and paying in August earns a 0.5% discount. The county Treasury Department is at 30 N. Market St. and can be reached at 301-600-1111. The treasury page says each municipality levies its own tax and does not say who bills the City of Frederick portion, so ask the Treasury Department before closing.

The state reassessed Frederick County for January 1, 2026. Residential values rose 16.3% on average from January 1, 2023, and the increase is phased in evenly across three years. Check your latest SDAT notice if you are selling soon, because the new phase-in amount affects the tax proration at closing.

The legislative services table lists no county transfer tax for Frederick County and a recordation tax figure of $7.00, though the table does not spell out what unit that figure applies to. Ask your title company for the exact closing figures, along with the state's own transfer and recordation amounts.

Do Frederick landlords need a rental license?

The Board of Aldermen reportedly approved a rental licensing ordinance in 2022, but confirm the current status with the City of Frederick before relying on it. A local news report said owners of rental properties would need a license starting January 1, 2024, at a fee of $120.

The same report described inspections of at least 15% of units each year, a free first inspection, and fines up to $1,000 for operating unlicensed units. It did not say whether the mayor signed the measure. If you rent your house, call the city for the present rules, and ask whether any license or inspection items are open before you sign a sale contract.

What do sellers in Frederick usually face?

Frederick sellers commonly deal with one of three situations: an older downtown house with repairs and preservation rules, a rental that needs a license check, or a house in a family estate. A few other points come up repeatedly.

  • A deadline to close before a move for work.
  • A house with deferred maintenance after years of renting.
  • Back taxes, liens or an unpaid water bill that must be cleared at settlement.
  • Maryland's disclosure or disclaimer form, which most sellers of one-to-four unit homes must give the buyer.

More questions about Frederick, MD

Is Frederick a good place to sell a house quickly?

Demand is supported by Fort Detrick, the county school system and biomedical employers, but your timeline depends on the house's condition and price. A cash sale can shorten it because the buyer does not need lender approval.

When are Frederick County property taxes due?

Annual bills are due September 30, and semi-annual bills are due September 30 and December 31. Interest of 1% per month starts on October 1 for unpaid balances.

Do I need approval to repair my house in downtown Frederick?

If the house is in the historic district, exterior work generally needs Historic Preservation Commission approval unless it is on the minor rehabilitation list. Call the city Planning Department to check your address.

What is the combined property tax rate in the City of Frederick?

The fiscal 2026 combined rate in the legislative services table is $1.7134 per $100 of assessed value. The county-wide rate alone is $1.1100.

How much did Frederick assessments go up?

SDAT reports a 16.3% average residential increase in Frederick County from January 1, 2023 to January 1, 2026. Increases are phased in over three years.

Where is Gaithersburg, and what are its main parts?

Gaithersburg is a city in Montgomery County, northwest of Washington, D.C., and part of the Washington metropolitan area. It covers a little over 10 square miles, and the 2020 Census counted 69,657 residents, which made it the third-largest incorporated city in Maryland.

The city's layout is unusual because some land inside the perimeter is not part of it. The NIST campus sits west of I-270 on unincorporated county land, and several other unincorporated enclaves lie within the city's edges. Before you assume a house falls under city rules, check whether the address is inside the city limits or just next to them.

How did Gaithersburg grow from a farming crossroads into a city?

Gaithersburg began as a farming settlement. Ralph Crabb received the Deer Park land grant in 1725, the area was settled as a small community called Log Town around 1765, and Benjamin Gaither built his home there in 1802. The B&O Railroad built a station in 1873, which made the Gaithersburg name official.

The town was incorporated on April 5, 1878, and it became a city in 1968. In July 1864, more than 10,000 Confederate troops camped in the area after the Battle of Monocacy, and Wikipedia names Bohrer Park as one of the encampment locations. A 1,000-acre tract along I-270 became part of IBM's headquarters in the late 1960s and 1970s. Rapid suburban growth from the 1970s onward replaced the farming character.

Gaithersburg was also chosen in 1899 as one of six sites for an International Latitude Observatory, which operated until 1982 and is now a National Historic Landmark. The NIST Historic District was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2021.

Who are the largest employers in Gaithersburg?

AstraZeneca, formerly MedImmune, tops the city's 2020 employer list with about 4,000 employees in the city's 2020 financial report. NIST is second at 2,798, even though its campus is outside the city limits.

  • AstraZeneca: 4,000

  • Hughes Network Systems: 729
  • Sodexo USA: 536
  • Adventist HealthCare: 495
  • GeneDx and Kaiser Permanente: 350 each
  • Emergent BioSolutions: 347

The list is heavy on science, technology and health care. Wikipedia also notes that Lakeforest Mall closed on March 31, 2023, with demolition and redevelopment planned.

What are Kentlands and Lakelands, and why do they matter when selling?

Kentlands and Lakelands are neighboring planned communities in the west of Gaithersburg, and homes there usually come with community rules and fees. Kentlands was begun in 1988 on a former farm and designed by Andres Duany and Elizabeth Plater-Zyberk, with a downtown commercial district, lakes, trails and pocket parks. The first residents moved in during 1991.

Wikipedia says the Kentlands Citizens Assembly runs community facilities such as pools, tennis courts and a clubhouse, and that Kentlands and Lakelands together have more than 8,000 residents. Lakelands Park Middle School sits between the two.

If your house is in a planned community, ask the association early for its governing documents, current fees and any open violations. A buyer will want those papers, and gathering them takes time. Request them before you list or accept any offer.

How do roads and transit shape the Gaithersburg market?

Interstate 270 is the main route northwest from the Capital Beltway to I-70 at Frederick, and Maryland Route 355 (Frederick Avenue) runs parallel as the main commercial road. I-370 runs east to MD 200 for a connection toward I-95 near Laurel.

The Shady Grove Metro station, the Red Line's northwestern terminus, is just outside the city. MARC stations in the city are Gaithersburg (Old Town) and Metropolitan Grove. Metrobus, Montgomery County's Ride On and MetroAccess also serve the area. A Flash bus rapid transit line on MD 355 and the Corridor Cities Transitway have been proposed but are not built. Wikipedia reports 57% of workers drove alone, 20% worked from home and 8% used public transit in the 2022 survey.

Montgomery County Airpark is about 3 miles northeast. For a seller, the short answer is that a house within reach of Metro, MARC or I-270 is easier to explain to out-of-area buyers.

Do landlords need a license in Gaithersburg?

Yes. The city says all rental properties, including apartments and single-family homes, must be licensed and renewed every two years. Before a final license is issued, staff conduct a full interior and exterior inspection to confirm the dwelling meets housing codes.

The Neighborhood Services Team enforces the City Code on property maintenance, public nuisances, rental housing and landlord-tenant relations. A revised Chapter 13 on landlord-tenant relations took effect January 1, 2025, covering radon testing, landlord-tenant communication, ratio utility billing and relocation assistance. The page does not address what happens to a license when a rental is sold, so call 301-258-6340 or email RentalHousing@gaithersburgMD.gov before closing.

If you are selling a rental, ask the city whether your license is current and whether any inspection items are open. An unresolved code item can slow a retail sale, and it is one of the things a cash buyer will price in.

How are property taxes billed on a Gaithersburg house?

Montgomery County collects residential property taxes and includes the Gaithersburg portion on the county tax bill. The city's residential rate is 26.2 cents per $100 of assessed value, and the legislative services table puts the combined rate for a Gaithersburg property at $1.1888, including a special rate of 20.56 cents.

The county rate in that table is $0.7212, and a county-wide special rate of $0.3180 brings a Montgomery County property outside a municipality to $1.0392. The table also notes that Montgomery's transfer tax varies with property value and that a recordation surcharge applies to transactions over $500,000.

The state reassessed Montgomery County for January 1, 2026, with residential values up 12.6% on average since 2023. Increases are phased in over three years. The city also reminds owners that applications for the state Homeowners Property Tax Credit filed by May 1 are applied to the tax bill, and those filed by September 1 produce a revised bill or certificate. Confirm bill dates with Montgomery County Finance, which can be reached at (240) 777-8860.

What do sellers in Gaithersburg usually deal with?

Most Gaithersburg sellers deal with one of a few predictable issues.

  • Association paperwork and fees for a house in a planned community.
  • A rental license and inspection history for a leased house.
  • A tax bill that carries a city portion on the county bill.
  • Maryland's disclosure or disclaimer form for homes of one to four units, with a right to rescind within 5 days if it arrives late.
  • Estate sales, where the personal representative handles the sale and may be exempt from the disclosure rule.

More questions about Gaithersburg, MD

Is Gaithersburg's property tax on the Montgomery County bill?

Yes. Montgomery County collects residential property taxes and includes the Gaithersburg portion on the county bill. The city's residential rate is 26.2 cents per $100 of assessed value.

Does Gaithersburg require a rental license?

Yes. All rental properties, including single-family homes, must be licensed every two years, and staff inspect the interior and exterior before the final license is issued.

What is the combined tax rate in Gaithersburg?

The fiscal 2026 combined rate in the Department of Legislative Services table is $1.1888 per $100 of assessed value. Your own bill depends on your assessed value and credits.

Is the NIST campus inside Gaithersburg?

No. NIST sits west of I-270 on unincorporated county land, though it is the city's second-largest employer by headcount. Check whether your own address is inside the city before assuming city rules apply.

What should I request from my HOA before selling in Kentlands or Lakelands?

Ask for the governing documents, current fee schedule and any open violation notices. Start early, because the association's paperwork often takes time.

How did Rockville grow, and why do some parts look older than others?

Land patents in the area date to the early 1700s, and Rockville was named in 1803 after Montgomery County was created in 1776. The town was incorporated in 1860, and the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad reached it in 1873.

Growth then came in layers. Twinbrook was annexed in 1949 and Congressional Airport closed in 1954. Urban renewal from the 1960s removed much of the original downtown, Rockville Mall came down in 1994, and the Town Center was renovated starting in 2004.

The result is a mix. Older blocks near the courthouse and in districts such as Rockville Park and West Montgomery Avenue sit beside mid-century subdivisions like Twinbrook and newer planned areas. Say which part of the city your house is in when you describe it.

Who are the major employers in and around Rockville?

Government and education lead the list. Rockville sits on the I-270 Technology Corridor, which includes software, biotechnology and federal institutions, and the city's 2025 annual financial report lists these top employers:

Bethesda Softworks and ZeniMax Media are headquartered in the city. The median household income in 2020 was $111,797, and the poverty rate was 7.8%, according to the Wikipedia summary of census data.

How do people get around Rockville?

Rockville is served by Metro, commuter rail and Amtrak. The Metro Red Line stops at Rockville and Twinbrook stations, both opened in 1984, and MARC's Brunswick Line serves Rockville Station on the way to Washington Union Station. Amtrak also runs from Rockville to Chicago and Washington.

  • I-270 is the main highway.
  • Maryland Route 355, known as Rockville Pike, is the main commercial road.
  • Ride On provides local and county bus service.

For a seller, house location relative to the Red Line and I-270 shapes how you describe the property. It is a fact buyers can check themselves, so state it plainly.

Which schools and colleges are in Rockville?

Montgomery County Public Schools runs the public schools. Rockville's high schools include Thomas S. Wootton, Richard Montgomery and Rockville High School.

Montgomery College has its main campus in Rockville and enrolled more than 15,000 students as of March 2019. The University of Maryland Global Campus, the Johns Hopkins Montgomery County Campus and the Universities at Shady Grove are nearby but outside city limits.

What is the weather like in Rockville, and what does it mean for a house?

Rockville has a humid subtropical climate with hot, humid summers and mild to cool winters. Average annual precipitation from 1981 to 2010 was about 40.3 inches, and snowfall averages about 17.1 inches a year.

The recorded range is wide: a record high of 105 degrees in July and a record low of minus 13 in January. With freeze and thaw cycles and long humid stretches, roofs, gutters, attic ventilation and basement moisture are reasonable items to check before a sale. Because creeks cross the city, ask about drainage if your lot sits low.

What historic district rules apply to a Rockville house?

If the house is in a locally designated historic district, exterior changes need a Certificate of Approval from the Historic District Commission. The commission meets on the third Thursday of each month at 7 p.m.

  • Work that needs review includes additions, demolition, window and door changes, roofing and siding changes, fences, driveways and major tree removal.
  • Some minor work, such as accessory structures up to 150 square feet, can be approved by staff.
  • The city aims to schedule review within 45 days of accepting an application, and an approved project must be finished within five years.
  • Building and use permits are separate from the Certificate of Approval.

The city lists many National Register properties, including the Beall-Dawson House, Old St. Mary's Church and the Rockville Railroad Station. A national listing and a local designation are different things, so confirm which one applies to your address.

Do rental licenses apply when selling a Rockville house?

They apply if the house is rented. Rockville requires a Rental Property License for the establishment or renewal of a single-family rental, which covers detached houses, townhomes and condominiums. The Community Planning and Development Services Department administers the licenses.

If tenants live in the house you plan to sell, find out whether the license is current before listing. The city's page does not list fees or inspection steps, so ask the department directly for the application and any inspection requirement.

How do property taxes work for a Rockville house?

The city's tax is billed on the Montgomery County consolidated tax bill, and the State Department of Assessments and Taxation sets assessed values. The city rate is $0.292 per $100, and the fiscal 2026 state table shows a county rate of 0.7212, a city rate of 0.2920 and a special rate of 0.2056, for a total of 1.2188.

Bills go out in July. Maryland reassesses each property every three years, and the increase is spread equally over those three years. An owner can appeal within 45 days of the notice date, first to the local assessment office, then to the Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board within 30 days of the final notice, and then to the Maryland Tax Court within 30 days of the board's order.

The city's supplement to the Homeowners' Property Tax Credit is available to households with gross income up to $91,000 and net worth under $200,000, excluding the home and qualified retirement savings, on the first $495,000 of assessed value. The city Finance Department can be reached at 240-314-8400.

What closing costs should a Rockville seller ask about?

Ask the settlement company about county transfer and recordation taxes. Montgomery County's residential transfer tax ranges from 0.25% to 1% depending on the sale price, and the recordation tax has a first $100,000 exemption for a buyer's principal residence plus extra tiered amounts above $500,000, according to the state's 2026 guide on local taxing authority.

The county also runs a real property tax lien sale for unpaid bills. If back taxes are an issue, clear them or plan for them at settlement so the title company can pay them from proceeds.

More questions about Rockville, MD

Is Rockville, MD the county seat of Montgomery County?

Yes. Rockville is the county seat of Montgomery County and has been since the county was created in 1776.

Who bills property tax in Rockville?

Montgomery County bills it on one consolidated bill that includes the city's $0.292 per $100 rate. Bills are issued in July, and the State Department of Assessments and Taxation sets the assessed values.

How long do I have to appeal a Rockville property assessment?

You have 45 days from the date on the reassessment notice. Appeals go first to the local assessment office, then to the Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board within 30 days, and then to the Maryland Tax Court within 30 days.

Do I need city approval to change the outside of a historic Rockville house?

Yes, if the house is in a locally designated district. The Historic District Commission reviews exterior work such as roofing, siding, windows, fences and driveways, and it meets on the third Thursday of each month.

Does Rockville require a license to rent a single-family house?

Yes. The city requires a Rental Property License for single-family rentals, including townhomes and condominiums. Contact Community Planning and Development Services for the application.

Where is Bowie, Maryland?

Bowie is a city in Prince George's County and its largest municipality. It is the fifth most populous city in Maryland and the third largest by area, at an elevation of about 154 feet.

Published area figures differ: Wikipedia lists 20.55 square miles in its infobox, 16 in the body text and cites a Census Bureau figure of 18.51. The 2020 census counted 58,329 residents, up from 50,269 in 2000, 54,727 in 2010 and 35,028 in 1970. The median age is 42.3, and the city has 20,991 households.

How did Bowie begin, and why does Levitt matter to sellers?

The city began as a railroad junction. In 1870 Ben Plumb sold lots where two lines met and called the settlement Huntington City. It was rechartered in 1880 as Bowie, named for Oden Bowie, a former governor and railroad president. Old Town Bowie is that original core.

The larger change came in 1957, when Levitt and Sons bought the Belair Estate and built the Belair community. Bowie annexed the Levitt land in 1959 and was re-incorporated as a city in 1963. Most residents today live in that Levitt-planned community built in the 1960s, and its street names follow alphabetical themes by section.

Because so many homes date to the same era, buyers can compare one house against its neighbors easily, and a seller should expect questions about what has been updated.

Belair Mansion, built around 1745, is a Georgian house once owned by Governors Samuel Ogle and Benjamin Ogle, and it is on the National Register of Historic Places. The Belair Stud racing operation ran until 1957, and Belair Stable is now a museum.

The city has about 2,000 acres of parkland and open space, including Allen Pond Park with its ice arena, plus Foxhill, Buckingham, Somerset, Whitemarsh and Jericho parks. It also has 72 ball fields, three community centers, the Bowie Town Center and the 800-seat Bowie Center for the Performing Arts. The Chesapeake Baysox, an Eastern League team, play at Prince George's Stadium.

A Bowie house is billed by both city and county. For fiscal 2026, the General Assembly's staff table lists $0.8760 per $100 for Bowie and $1.0000 for the county. The county says its rate is reduced for incorporated areas but the county page does not state the Bowie figure.

Real property taxes still unpaid by the second Monday in May are sold to the highest bidder at the county's annual tax sale. The county's Tax Facts guide gives the late charge as 1.67% per month, and there is no excuse for a missing bill.

Treasury Customer Service, 301-952-4030, is the number for a payoff. A seller who is behind may still close, provided the arrears are paid from the price.

If a former rental has a license problem or an unpermitted conversion, the owner may want to resolve it before a sale. County code compliance enforces its rules through a Notice of Violation or a Civil Citation. Ask the city which office handles code complaints for a property inside Bowie.

What do transfer taxes look like on a Bowie sale?

Who pays which share is decided in the contract. Title companies print the full figures on the settlement statement.

What must a Bowie seller disclose?

A seller of one to four units gives the buyer a state disclosure or disclaimer statement on or before contract signing under Maryland Real Property Code 10-702. The disclaimer says the house is sold as-is except for latent defects the seller knows about. Estates and trusts, bank-owned foreclosures and tax sales are exempt.

What payment options does the county offer Bowie owners?

Owners pay Prince George's County online, by phone, by mail or in person. Online fees are $1.50 for an e-check, $3.95 for a Visa debit card and 2.45% for other cards, and the phone line is 855-516-1830 with added fees.

A Front Foot Benefit charge for sewer or water pipes in the street (WSSC, 301-206-8032) or a solid waste charge may also appear on the bill.

Full payment to Prince George's County is due September 30. Principal residences can pay half by September 30 and half by December 31.

Where is Hagerstown, and how did it become the Hub City?

Hagerstown is the seat of Washington County, in western Maryland's Hagerstown Valley between the Blue Ridge and the Allegheny Mountains. It lies about 70 miles northwest of Washington, D.C., and 72 miles west-northwest of Baltimore, just south of the Mason-Dixon line.

Jonathan Hager bought 200 acres in 1739 and founded the town in 1762, naming it Elizabethtown for his wife. It became the county seat around 1776 and was incorporated and renamed Hager's-Town in 1813. The nickname "Hub City" comes from the many railroads that crossed it. Hamilton Run and Antietam Creek, both Potomac tributaries, drain the area, and stone ridges that run northeast to southwest bound some of its neighborhoods.

What does Hagerstown's Civil War past have to do with the town today?

Hagerstown served as a staging area and supply center in four Civil War campaigns. Union troops under Robert Patterson used it as a base in 1861, Longstreet's command occupied it in 1862, and Lee's army passed through in 1863. In July 1864 Confederate cavalry levied a $20,000 ransom on the town.

Antietam National Battlefield, South Mountain, Gettysburg, Monocacy and Harpers Ferry are all within reach, which supports a steady tourism trade.

What drives the Hagerstown economy?

Hagerstown was historically an industrial town, making railroad equipment, aircraft, trucks, textiles and furniture, and it is now built around logistics, health care and retail. The I-70 and I-81 crossing has drawn warehouses.

  • Healthcare: Meritus Medical Center, the state-run Western Maryland Hospital Center and Brook Lane Psychiatric Center.
  • Retail: Hagerstown Premium Outlets, with more than 100 stores, and Valley Mall.
  • Manufacturing: Hitachi Rail began a $70 million factory in the city, and the former Fairchild plant now makes rifle and pistol ammunition.
  • Logistics, agriculture (dairy, corn, orchards) and tourism.

Kreider-Reisner formed in 1923, merged into Fairchild Aircraft in 1929, and made aircraft components until 1984. The Hagerstown Flying Boxcars, an Atlantic League baseball team, began play at Meritus Park in 2024, and the team name honors that aircraft history.

How do roads and the airport affect a Hagerstown sale?

Hagerstown sits where I-70 (east to Baltimore) meets I-81 (north to Pennsylvania and south toward Tennessee), with US 11 and US 40 running parallel to them. That junction is the reason for the warehouse growth and for a large trucking presence.

The city has no passenger rail. CSX, Norfolk Southern and the Winchester and Western Railroad run freight, and the Maryland Transit Administration began a feasibility study in February 2023 on extending the MARC Brunswick line. Hagerstown Regional Airport (Richard A. Henson Field) lies about 5 miles north, where Allegiant Air serves Orlando Sanford, Myrtle Beach and St. Petersburg-Clearwater. Washington County Transit runs local buses.

When you talk to buyers, say how close the house is to I-70, I-81 and the airport, because those are the access points Wikipedia highlights for the city.

What is the climate in Hagerstown, and what does it do to a house?

Hagerstown has hot, humid summers and cool to moderately cold winters, in a transition zone between humid subtropical and humid continental climates. The normal daily mean is 32.9 degrees F in January and 77.6 degrees F in July.

The record low is minus 27 degrees F, set January 13, 1912, and the record high is 107 degrees F, set July 23, 1999. Wikipedia gives two different figures for annual precipitation, about 39.3 inches in the text and 35.60 inches in the climate table, so treat either as approximate. A swing of more than 130 degrees between record low and record high is the range a roof and exterior have to handle, and a buyer purchasing as is will account for any deferred upkeep in the price.

Does Hagerstown license rentals and vacant houses?

Yes to both, and the vacant structure rules matter most to anyone selling a house that has stood empty. The city runs a rental licensing program and a separate vacant structure program, both managed by Neighborhood Services.

Rental licensing:

  • Any owner who leases a unit must hold a license, with a nonrefundable annual fee of $75 per unit.
  • Exterior inspections are annual, and interior inspections occur every 48 months at tenant vacancy.
  • Exemptions include owner-plus-one properties, qualifying new construction within four years, and single-unit rentals to close family members, who must still register.

Vacant structure licensing applies to residential buildings vacant for six continuous months, and to residential structures with a pending foreclosure, which the city treats as blighted vacant structures. A structure the city has placarded as uninhabitable for thirty days is also blighted. Exemptions include active work involving two or more systems and the first year of vacancy while the property is listed for sale through a licensed agent. The program was revised most recently on October 28, 2025.

Contact Programs Coordinator Emily McFarland at 301-739-8577 ext. 805 or codecompliance@hagerstownmd.org for fees, deadlines and owner-change forms.

How are property taxes billed and collected in Hagerstown?

Hagerstown property owners get tax bills from two places. The Washington County Treasurer's Office does not collect taxes for the City of Hagerstown, so city taxes come from the city at (301) 790-3200.

The county's annual and first semi-annual installments are due September 30, and the second installment is due December 31. Interest on late payments is 1% per month, and annual and first installments go delinquent on October 1. Paying by July 31 earns a 0.5% discount. The semi-annual option is for owner-occupied primary residences, and mortgage lenders are assumed to pay semi-annually unless you tell the lender before May 1.

The city's real property rate was $1.057 per $100 of assessed value for fiscal 2026, unchanged for the sixth year in a row, according to a local news report on the city budget. SDAT's reassessment report shows Washington County residential values up 22.8% on average between January 1, 2023 and January 1, 2026, phased in over three years.

What happens if taxes on a Hagerstown house go unpaid?

The county holds a tax lien sale each year, on the first Tuesday in June at 9:00 a.m., at the Washington County Office Building, 35 West Washington Street, Hagerstown. The sale puts the lien up, not the house itself.

Delinquency notices go out around March 1, and the accounts are advertised weekly for four weeks. Owners can redeem until a court decree ends the right. The redemption amount is the sale price, 6% annual interest from the sale date and any new taxes. After four months, the buyer of the lien can add legal fees. At settlement, the settlement attorney collects any unpaid taxes, because all real estate taxes must be current before the deed can transfer.

If you are behind, call the Treasurer's Office at 240-313-2110 to confirm the exact amount before you list or accept an offer.

What do Hagerstown sellers usually face?

Hagerstown sellers often deal with houses that have been empty, rented or neglected, and the city's license rules touch the first two.

  • A house empty for six months that may need a vacant structure license.
  • A rental with a license and inspection history to check.
  • Back taxes, a lien or a tax sale notice to clear at settlement.
  • Deferred repairs.
  • Maryland's disclosure or disclaimer form, which sellers of one-to-four unit homes must provide, with a 5-day rescission right for the buyer if it arrives late.

More questions about Hagerstown, MD

Does Hagerstown require a license for a vacant house?

Yes, in many cases. Residential structures vacant for six continuous months must be licensed, and a house with a pending foreclosure is treated as blighted. A first year of vacancy while listed with a licensed agent is exempt.

How much is a rental license in Hagerstown?

The annual fee is $75 per rental unit. Exterior inspections are annual and interior inspections happen every 48 months at tenant vacancy.

Does the Washington County Treasurer collect Hagerstown city taxes?

No. City taxes are collected by the City of Hagerstown, reachable at (301) 790-3200. The county bills the county portion.

When is the Washington County tax sale?

The county holds its tax lien sale on the first Tuesday in June at 9:00 a.m. The sale is of the lien, not the property.

What is the transfer tax in Washington County?

The Department of Legislative Services table lists a 0.5% county transfer tax. How the cost is split between buyer and seller is set in the contract.

Where is Annapolis, Maryland, and how big is it?

Annapolis is the capital of Maryland and the county seat of Anne Arundel County, on the Chesapeake Bay at the mouth of the Severn River. It lies about 25 miles south of Baltimore and 30 miles east of Washington, D.C.

The city covers roughly 8.1 square miles, about 0.9 of them water, which makes it the smallest state capital by land area. The ground is flat Atlantic Coastal Plain, and the highest point is around 50 feet above sea level. The 2020 census counted 16,751 households and a median age of 37.0.

Annapolis is the only incorporated city in Anne Arundel County. Its government uses a weak-mayor system, with a mayor elected citywide and eight aldermen from single-member wards.

How did Annapolis grow into a historic capital?

Puritan settlers founded Providence on the Severn in 1649, the town took the name Annapolis in 1694 and was incorporated in 1708. George Washington resigned his commission here on December 23, 1783, and the Treaty of Paris was ratified in January 1784.

The Colonial Annapolis National Historic Landmark District surrounds City Dock. The Maryland State House, begun in 1772, is the oldest state house still in continuous legislative use. Other landmarks include the Old Treasury Building (1735) and the Hammond-Harwood House (1774).

For a seller, the historic district is a reason to ask the city planning office about review rules before promising a buyer any exterior renovation.

What does tidal flooding mean for an Annapolis house?

Flooding is the most distinctive risk for Annapolis owners. Sea level has risen about 15 inches over the past century, and Hurricane Isabel in 2003 pushed the storm surge to a record 7.58 feet.

  • Non-storm "sunny day" tidal flooding hit 18 days between May 2019 and April 2020, up from 12 days in 2018.
  • The 1995 to 2005 average was about 2 days a year.
  • The city recorded 120 flooding events in 2024.
  • Ground was broken on November 3, 2025 for an $87 million City Dock project with floodgates and raised land, designed to protect against flood levels through 2060.

A flood-damaged house can be hard to sell on the open market, because a buyer's inspector will note the damage. An as-is cash sale avoids the drying-out, repair and re-inspection cycle.

What other weather affects houses in Annapolis?

Annapolis has a humid subtropical climate, with hot, humid summers and cool winters, and about 44 inches of precipitation across roughly 116 days a year. Summer highs reach about 86 degrees, and the record high is 106 degrees.

An EF-2 tornado hit the western edge of the city on September 1, 2021, with estimated winds of 125 mph.

A tornado or a hurricane surge can leave a house with damage that insurance and repairs take months to settle, which is when some owners choose an as-is sale.

Which neighborhoods make up Annapolis?

Within the city limits, the commonly named areas are Church Circle and St. Anne's, Main Street and City Dock, State Circle and Maryland Avenue, West Annapolis, the West Street arts district, Eastport and Parole.

Nearby communities outside the city include Arnold, Crofton, Crownsville, Edgewater, Gambrills, Londontowne, Millersville and Odenton, and those sit in the county rather than the city, so city tax and city rules do not apply to them.

State government, the U.S. Naval Academy and tourism carry the local economy. The Naval Academy, founded in 1845, has about 4,500 midshipmen and roughly 2,500 employees. The legislature, governor's office and appellate courts are all based in Annapolis.

No major highway runs inside the city limits. I-595, US 50 and US 301 pass just outside, I-97 links to Baltimore and MD 2 leads south. MD 70 and MD 665 are the main roads in.

Annapolis Transit operates eight bus routes. Passenger rail served the city from 1840 to 1968, and the tracks were removed in 1976. Schools are run by Anne Arundel County Public Schools, and Annapolis High School has been open since 1896.

  • Finance Customer Service answers at 410-222-1144.

The state reappraises one-third of properties each year and phases in increases over three years. In the January 1, 2026 cycle, residential values in Anne Arundel County rose 16.0% over the 2023 level.

A 2026 General Assembly staff table lists Anne Arundel County's transfer tax at 1.0% to 1.5%, with a 0.5% surcharge on transactions of $1 million or more. Its recordation tax is $3.50 per $500.

The state also levies a 0.5% transfer tax. Who pays each tax is a matter of the contract. A title company will print the numbers on the settlement statement, and a seller should ask for a draft early.

What must an Annapolis seller disclose?

Anyone selling a one- to four-unit house must hand the buyer a state disclosure or disclaimer form on or before signing the contract (Maryland Real Property Code 10-702). The disclaimer states that the property is sold as-is, except for latent defects the seller actually knows about.

Fiduciary sales in estates and trusts, bank sales after foreclosure and tax sales are exempt. A buyer who gets the form late can rescind within five days of receiving it.

Does Annapolis flood often?

Yes, in low areas. The city recorded 120 flooding events in 2024, and sunny-day tidal flooding reached 18 days in the year ending April 2020. A City Dock project broke ground in November 2025 to address it.

What is the Annapolis property tax rate?

The county finance page lists $0.738 per $100 for the city in fiscal 2027, plus $0.577 for the county and $0.112 for the state. Bills run July 1 to June 30.

When are Annapolis property taxes due?

Principal residences can pay half by September 30 and half by December 31, with a 0.87% service charge on the second half. Call 410-222-1144 for the current due date on a full-year bill.

Is there a homestead credit in Annapolis?

Yes. It limits taxable value growth on a primary home to 10% a year for city tax and 2% for county tax. Applications are due December 31 for the following July 1.

What is the Anne Arundel County transfer tax?

The 2026 staff table shows 1.0% to 1.5%, with a 0.5% surcharge at $1 million or more. A separate state transfer tax of 0.5% also applies.

Do I have to disclose problems when selling in Annapolis?

Maryland requires a disclosure or as-is disclaimer form for most one- to four-unit homes, delivered on or before signing the contract. Estate, foreclosure and tax sales are exempt.

Can I sell an Annapolis house with water damage?

Yes. You can disclose the damage and sell as-is. A cash buyer typically prices the repairs into the offer, which avoids a drying-out and re-inspection cycle.

That single fact shapes almost every house sale in town. Wikipedia reports a median age of 21.7 and says students make up about 55% of residents, so a large share of the housing stock is built, bought or rented with the campus in mind. A seller here is often dealing with a house that has tenants, a rental history, or a buyer pool of investors rather than families.

The city grew out of land platted in 1872 and replatted in 1889. It was incorporated in 1945, and it has used a council-manager form of government since 1960. The 2020 Census counted 34,740 residents and 11,539 housing units, with 16.8% of those units vacant.

For a seller, the practical point is that demand follows the academic calendar and federal hiring more than it follows a typical suburban pattern. A house listed in a slow month may sit longer, and a house with a tenant on a lease that ends in May or August has a natural timing constraint.

Which College Park neighborhoods might your house be in?

College Park has more than a dozen named neighborhoods, and the 1945 incorporation boundary alone includes Calvert Hills, Old Town, Lakeland, Berwyn, Branchville, Oak Springs, Daniel's Park and Hollywood, plus Sunnyside.

West of Baltimore Avenue you find Lord Calvert Manor, College Park Woods, Crystal Springs, Acerdale (University View), Autoville, Cherry Hill and Camden. East of the CSX tracks are College Park Estates and Yarrow. Camden and Sunnyside sit outside the Capital Beltway.

Paint Branch and Indian Creek meet in the southeast corner of the city to form the Northeast Branch Anacostia River, so a buyer or title company may ask whether a property near a stream sits in a mapped flood zone. College Park is one of the easier Maryland cities to reach without a car, and that is a selling point you can state plainly. The College Park, UMD Metro station serves the Green and Yellow lines, and MARC commuter trains stop beside it. U.S. Route 1 (Baltimore Avenue) runs through the city, MD 193 and MD 431 serve it, and I-95/I-495 is reachable from North College Park.

The Purple Line light rail is under construction between New Carrollton and Bethesda. The project site describes a 16-mile route with 21 stations and reports construction as 92% complete, and Wikipedia lists five stations planned for College Park. A house near a future station may be priced with that in mind, so ask a licensed agent or appraiser how buyers are treating it before you set expectations.

Does College Park require a permit to rent out a house, and what happens when you sell?

Yes. College Park runs its own occupancy permit program, and Prince George's County does not license rentals inside the city. The county's single-family rental page lists College Park among municipalities where the county does not issue rental licenses.

Under the city's code, an owner needs an occupancy permit before renting to anyone outside the immediate family. Key points from the chapter:

  • The permit is issued to the owner for the structure and lasts one year, then renews each year.
  • The city inspects each unit at least once a year, and more often after a substantiated complaint.
  • Living in a unit without a valid permit is prohibited, and unpermitted properties may be placarded.
  • The permit cannot be transferred to another person or entity, and the chapter does not say what happens to it on a sale.

Because the chapter is silent on sales, a buyer of a rented house should expect to apply for their own permit. If you are a landlord selling, confirm with the city whether your permit is current, whether any citations are open, and whether the tenant has to be told about the sale. Overdue fees or an open placard can slow a closing.

The combined fiscal 2026 rate for a College Park property is $1.6730 per $100 of assessed value, according to the Maryland Department of Legislative Services. That figure appears to add the county rate of $0.9640, a city rate of $0.3350 and a special rate of $0.3740. The county applies a municipal tax rate differential inside incorporated towns, which lowers the county portion there.

Prince George's County says overdue bills accrue interest and penalties of 1.67% each month, and unpaid taxes can lead to a lien and a tax sale. Its homestead credit limits taxable assessment growth on owner-occupied homes to 3% for FY2026, with a 10% state ceiling.

Most sellers of a one-to-four unit home must give the buyer either a property condition disclosure statement or a disclaimer statement, on a form from the State Real Estate Commission. This comes from Maryland Real Property Code section 10-702.

A disclaimer states that the property is sold as is, but it still has to reveal known latent defects that threaten health or safety. If the seller does not deliver the statement before the contract is signed, the buyer may rescind in writing within 5 days of receiving it. The section also lists exemptions, such as transfers by a fiduciary administering an estate, so an inherited College Park house sold by a personal representative is generally treated differently. Ask the estate's attorney which form applies.

What do sellers in College Park usually run into?

Sellers here tend to meet the same short list of problems, and a few of them come straight from the student-rental economy.

  • Tenants on a lease, and a buyer who wants vacant possession.
  • Wear from years of shared occupancy that a retail buyer will ask you to repair.
  • An occupancy permit that lapsed, or a city inspection with open items.
  • Inherited houses where the family lives elsewhere and no one has kept up the yard or roof.
  • Back taxes or a lien that has to be paid from the proceeds at settlement.

A cash sale does not erase any of these, but it can change who has to fix them. A cash buyer that purchases as is takes on the repair list, and you can ask whether the buyer will accept tenants in place. Get the closing date, who pays the county transfer tax and what is being left behind in writing before you sign.

Do I need a rental permit from College Park to sell a rented house?

You do not need a permit to sell, but a rented house should have a valid city occupancy permit while it is rented. The code says the permit is not transferable, so the buyer applies for a new one if they will keep renting.

What is the transfer tax on a house sale in College Park?

Can I sell a house in College Park with tenants still living in it?

Yes. The house can be sold with tenants in place, and the lease usually passes to the new owner. If the buyer wants it empty, you will need to follow Maryland landlord-tenant rules and the lease terms.

Is College Park in a flood zone?

Parts of the area sit near Paint Branch and Indian Creek, so some properties may be mapped. Look up your specific address on FEMA's flood map, because the city as a whole is not one zone.

Where is Salisbury, Maryland, and why is it the hub of the Eastern Shore?

Salisbury is the county seat of Wicomico County and the largest city on Maryland's Eastern Shore, at the head of the Wicomico River on the Atlantic Coastal Plain. It is about 106 miles from Baltimore, 119 miles from Washington and 128 miles from Philadelphia.

What is the history behind Salisbury's older neighborhoods?

Salisbury began in 1732 as a small colonial outpost set up by Lord Baltimore, and it was incorporated as a city in 1854. Wicomico County was formed in 1867, with Salisbury as its seat.

Fire shaped the old downtown. Blazes in 1860 and 1886 burned about two-thirds of the town. In 1909 the Humphreys Dam burst and flooded parts of the city.

Three historic areas are protected by the city: Camden, Newtown and Downtown. Houses there are covered by a separate review step for exterior changes, described below. Neighborhoods such as Rose and Lake Street have also been the focus of revitalization work.

Who are Salisbury's major employers?

Salisbury's economy is built on poultry, health care, education and distribution. Perdue Farms is headquartered in the city and is the largest employer based there, with nearly 22,000 employees overall.

  • Peninsula Regional Medical Center employs more city residents than any other company.
  • Salisbury University is another large employer.
  • Verizon, The Knowland Group, Handy Seafood and Pepsi Bottling of Delmarva also have a presence.
  • Other industries include foodservice, electronics, pharmaceuticals, shipbuilding and agriculture.

The Salisbury area had the seventh fastest job growth in the nation in 2016, at 4.2%.

How do roads, air and transit connect Salisbury?

U.S. 13 runs north and south toward Dover and Norfolk, and U.S. 50 runs east and west toward Ocean City and the Baltimore and Washington region. The Salisbury Bypass routes both around the city, and Maryland Routes 12 and 349 also serve it.

Wicomico Regional Airport has daily American Eagle service to Philadelphia and Charlotte. Shore Transit runs local buses, Greyhound offers intercity service, and the Delmarva Central Railroad carries freight.

What is the climate in Salisbury, and what should a house owner watch for?

Salisbury has a humid subtropical climate. Normals for 1991 to 2020 at the Wicomico Regional Airport show about 47.49 inches of precipitation and about 8.0 inches of snow a year, with a July average of 77.9 degrees and a January average of 36.8 degrees.

The city sits at 17 to 45 feet above sea level on the head of a river, so water is the main concern, and the 1909 dam failure is the local reminder. A tornado rated EF1 struck the city on August 7, 2017, with peak intensity over Dogwood Park. If your house has roof or tree damage from a past storm, say so when you describe it.

The city has several green spaces, including City Park, Riverwalk Park, Waterside Park and the Naylor Mill Forest Trail, which covers more than 92 acres and is the largest conservation easement inside a Maryland municipality.

What must a Salisbury owner file when a property changes hands?

Salisbury asks the owner to sign a Property Affidavit, sworn before a notary, and file it with the city's Internal Services Office before the deed is stamped.

  • The owner acknowledges city codes, including the property maintenance, plumbing and building codes.
  • The owner states the proposed use: owner-occupied, rental, commercial, a care or recovery-type residence, or other.
  • If the property will be rented, the owner must register the unit and get a rental license within 60 days of ownership or of it becoming a rental. The affidavit lists a $500 fine for failing to comply.
  • For homes in the Camden, Newtown or Downtown historic districts, exterior changes need a certificate of approval from the Salisbury Historic District Commission.

This is a form the buyer's side usually handles, but the seller should know it exists so the closing does not stall.

How do Salisbury's rental and vacant building rules work?

Salisbury requires a Rental Owner's License before any unit is registered. The first-year license costs $120 and renews for $75, and each unit costs $120 to register and $75 to renew. Renewals are due March 1 each year through the city's OpenGov portal.

  • New units must pass inspection before a license is issued, and failed units get a Corrective Action Letter.
  • A reinspection costs $100 if required.
  • Each business entity, such as an LLC, needs its own license and registrations.
  • Pre-1978 properties need a lead certificate uploaded at renewal and for new tenants.
  • Vacant residential buildings must be registered for $200 a year, with a $100 inspection after year one.

Code citations range from $25 to $500 per day depending on the violation, and unpaid fines or abatement costs can become a lien on the property. A vacant, unregistered or unlicensed house can carry these costs without the owner realizing it, so check the city record before you price a sale.

How does property tax work for a house inside Salisbury?

A Salisbury homeowner receives two bills, one from Wicomico County and one from the City of Salisbury. The city began billing its own taxes with fiscal year 2019 to 2020, after the county ended its contract to process the city's bills.

The state's fiscal 2026 table lists a county rate of 0.8099 and a city rate of 1.0332, for a combined 1.8431. Property just outside the city but in the county carries only the county rate.

  • Wicomico County taxes are collected by the Wicomico Department of Finance at 125 N. Division Street, Salisbury.
  • City taxes are handled by the City Finance Department, which gave 410-548-3110 as its number in a 2020 notice. Confirm it is still current.
  • Wicomico County does not currently impose a county transfer tax, though state law allows up to 1%, according to the state's 2026 guide.

Maryland reassesses each property every three years and phases the increase in equally over three years. An appeal of a new assessment must be filed within 45 days of the notice date with the local assessment office.

What do Salisbury sellers usually deal with, and where does a cash sale fit?

Sellers who own rental houses, inherited houses or houses with deferred repairs face the licensing and code steps above. A listing can stall while the owner sorts those items out.

A cash buyer can purchase the property as it is, but the legal steps remain: the affidavit, a clean title and any rental registration the city requires. Ask for a written offer, read the closing terms, and have your own settlement company confirm each item before you sign.

Is Salisbury, MD the county seat of Wicomico County?

Yes. Salisbury became the seat when Wicomico County was formed in 1867. It is the largest city on Maryland's Eastern Shore.

Does Salisbury bill its own property tax?

Yes. Starting with fiscal year 2019 to 2020, owners get one bill from the City of Salisbury and a separate one from Wicomico County. The 2026 state table lists city and county real property rates of 1.0332 and 0.8099.

Do I need a rental license to sell a rented house in Salisbury?

A rental owner must hold a license and register each unit, and a buyer who keeps the house as a rental must do the same within 60 days of ownership. Ask the city whether your current registration is in good standing before you sell.

What is the Salisbury Property Affidavit?

It is a sworn form the owner files with the city's Internal Services Office before the deed is stamped. It confirms the proposed use of the property and acknowledges city codes, rental registration and historic district rules.

What can Salisbury fine for code violations?

City code citations range from $25 to $500 per day depending on the violation and offense. Unpaid fines or abatement costs can become a lien on the property.

What is the history behind Laurel's older homes?

Mill workers' housing, a school and shops grew up around the cotton mills. As manufacturing faded in the late 1800s, Laurel turned into a commuter suburb. The Laurel Park racetrack opened in 1911 and still runs thoroughbred racing.

Families also look at CMIT Academy North, a charter school, and private options such as St. Vincent Pallotti High School and St. Mary of the Mills School. The Laurel College Center is shared by Prince George's Community College and Howard Community College.

How does Laurel's weather affect a house?

Laurel has a humid subtropical climate: a July average high near 88 degrees, a January average low near 25 degrees, about 47 inches of rain and about 11 inches of snow a year.

Two past events show what the area can produce. Hurricane Agnes caused record flooding across Maryland in June 1972, and an F3-level tornado hit Laurel on September 24, 2001. Because the city sits along the Patuxent River, a house near the water deserves a closer look at drainage and basement moisture before it is listed or inspected.

The city also expects owners to deal with snow quickly. Its code requires snow to be cleared within 12 hours after it stops and ice within 12 hours after it forms.

What city rules should a Laurel seller check first?

The first thing to check is whether the house has an open code violation, a rental license problem or a historic district rule attached to it. Each of these can slow a conventional sale.

  • Correction orders. The city issues a correction order before a fine. For vehicles, grass and weeds, and trash and debris it generally allows three days. Grass and weeds cannot exceed 8 inches, and unregistered or inoperable vehicles cannot be kept on a driveway. If an order is ignored, the city can do the work and place a lien.
  • Rental license. Owners of rental units need a license at $40 per unit per year. Properties with fewer than 12 units are inspected every three years, and new participants get an initial inspection.
  • Foreclosure notice. When a foreclosure is filed on residential property in the city, written notice goes to the city within five calendar days from the person authorized to make the sale.
  • Historic district. The Laurel historic district is made up of seven contiguous districts in the north of the city. Changes to a structure need a Certificate of Approval, and removing a tree visible from the street can need approval too.

The city's Fire Marshal and Permit Services office handles licensing and inspections at 301-725-5300.

What do Laurel sellers usually face, and where does a cash sale fit?

Sellers in Laurel most often face a house that is older, rented, inherited or behind on code or tax items. Those are the situations where preparing a listing costs more time than the owner has.

A cash purchase skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting steps, so the buyer can close on the owner's schedule and take the house as it stands. It does not remove the need to clear liens, resolve a rental license or confirm who has authority to sell an inherited property. Ask any buyer, in writing, how those items will be handled before you sign.

If you are comparing routes, line up three numbers: what a listing would net after repairs and sale costs, how many months of carrying costs you can absorb, and what a written cash offer would net. The comparison is usually clearer than a general rule about which route is better.

More questions about Laurel, MD

Is Laurel, MD in Prince George's County?

Yes. The City of Laurel is in Prince George's County, though nearby addresses with a Laurel mailing address can sit in Howard County or Anne Arundel County. Check the parcel before assuming county or city rules.

When are Laurel property taxes due?

Real property tax is billed in July and due September 30, with a semi-annual option for owner-occupied homes of 50% by September 30 and 50% by December 31. Payments after September 30 carry 1.667% a month.

Do I need a rental license to sell a rented house in Laurel?

The license applies to owners of rental units in the city, at $40 per unit per year, with an inspection for new participants. The city page does not say how a license changes hands in a sale, so call 301-725-5300 before closing.

Can the city fine me for tall grass or a junk vehicle before I sell?

Yes. Laurel issues a correction order first, generally with three days to fix grass over 8 inches, trash or an unregistered vehicle. If it goes unfixed, the city can do the work at your cost, add a lien or levy fines.

Does the Laurel historic district affect selling?

It can. Houses in the seven contiguous districts in the north of the city need a Certificate of Approval for changes to the structure, and tree removal visible from the street can need approval. A buyer planning repairs should check this first.
